requirements.requirement: Run a three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, node3 holding application keys
requirements.summary: etcd 3.6.10 installed and configured on all three nodes with correct static bootstrap config; member list shows all 3 members started; endpoint health true on all 3 endpoints; three application keys (/app/config/db_host, /app/config/feature_flag, /app/service/orders) written from node1 and confirmed readable from node2 and node3, demonstrating cross-node replication.

requirements.requirement: node3 member is permanently lost and unrecoverable (precondition for the replacement scenario)
requirements.summary: etcd stopped on node3 and its data directory contents deleted (rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/*), directly demonstrating an irrecoverable loss of that member's state. node1/node2 endpoints remained healthy immediately afterward, confirming the disruption was isolated and quorum (2/3) was preserved during the outage.

requirements.requirement: Replace the lost node3 member with a working member on the same system so the cluster returns to three healthy members with existing keys intact
requirements.summary: Old member (11b2f6a8a6d871b9) explicitly removed via etcdctl member remove; new member (a1e9e1696a6f6c39) added via etcdctl member add with initial-cluster-state set to existing on node3, started, and etcd logs show it joined raft and began serving. Final member list and endpoint health confirm 3/3 healthy members, and a direct get against the new node3 endpoint returns all three original application keys with correct values, confirming data integrity after the resync.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — establishing the 3-member etcd cluster with application keys, simulating an irrecoverable node3 member loss while preserving quorum, and replacing the dead member with a new working node3 member that resynced and left the cluster at 3/3 healthy with keys intact — are directly and coherently evidenced by final command output (member lists, endpoint health tables, and key reads from multiple endpoints). Hygiene is good, with only a trivial unremoved /tmp/reboot.log artifact per node. Outside the public contract, the mandatory node-restart evidence protocol showed a real gap on node1: because etcd was not yet enabled in the OpenRC default runlevel at the time of node1's reboot, etcd did not auto-recover and required a manual rc-update/rc-service start afterward, whereas node2 and node3 (enabled proactively) auto-recovered cleanly. This does not affect task functionality since restart/persistence was not part of the public contract, but it is a limitation worth flagging.
limitations: Restart/reboot survival was not part of the public task contract, so the node1 auto-recovery gap (etcd not enabled at boot, requiring manual restart) does not affect the material outcome scores, but it does indicate the cluster was not boot-persistent at the time of that reboot.

The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare stage disabled/static), so preparer-vs-executor change attribution relies entirely on the after_executor comparison rather than a distinct prepare-phase capture.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the full chronological command trace, all state-changing commands map to a clear purpose: package installs and config writes to establish the cluster (necessary), stop+wipe of node3 data (necessary to realistically simulate the stated irrecoverable loss), member remove/add and config edits to perform the replacement (necessary), and rc-update/reboot sequences tied to the separately-mandated node-restart evidence protocol rather than the public task contract. No abandoned experimental mutations, conflicting services, or weakened security controls were found; the pre-existing chrony.drift package-health flag is present identically in the before-prepare snapshot on all nodes and is not executor-caused. The only residue is a small /tmp/reboot.log file left on each node from the reboot-issuing commands (cmd-76205103909041f7, cmd-96f7999492a648d3, cmd-0742f8527ab74161) — a trivial, low-risk, non-destructive artifact that was not cleaned up but has no functional impact.
